subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Emerging economies are attractive to MNCs largely because they offer:
options: Shrinking populations and falling incomes
Fast-growing markets and often lower production costs
An absence of any local competition
Guaranteed political stability in all cases
questions.explain: Rapid growth, rising incomes and lower costs make emerging economies appealing for both sales and production.

questions.q: A common criticism of MNCs' impact on host countries is that they may:
options: Pay wages far above the local average to all staff
Use their power to exploit cheap labour, avoid taxes or damage the local environment
Refuse to repatriate any profits
Always strengthen local rivals' competitiveness
questions.explain: Critics argue MNCs can exploit low-cost labour, shift profits to avoid tax, and harm local environments and firms.

questions.q: Transfer pricing is a method by which MNCs may:
options: Increase wages for overseas workers
Set ethical prices for all customers
Eliminate exchange-rate risk entirely
Shift profits between subsidiaries in different countries to reduce their overall tax bill
questions.explain: Transfer pricing involves manipulating internal prices between subsidiaries to move profits to low-tax jurisdictions.

questions.q: Globalisation is best described as:
options: A government policy to restrict imports
The breakup of multinational companies
The increasing integration and interdependence of economies through trade, investment and technology
The decline of international trade between nations
questions.explain: Globalisation is the growing economic integration of national economies through trade, capital flows, migration and technology.

questions.q: Bartlett and Ghoshal's 'transnational' strategy attempts to:
options: Achieve global efficiency and strong local responsiveness simultaneously
Ignore both cost efficiency and local needs
Standardise everything with no local adaptation
Operate only in the firm's home country
questions.explain: A transnational strategy seeks both global cost efficiency and high local responsiveness at the same time.

questions.q: A strong (appreciating) domestic currency tends to:
options: Always increase a country's trade surplus
Have no effect on importers or exporters
Make imports cheaper and exports more expensive abroad
Make imports more expensive and exports cheaper
questions.explain: An appreciating currency lowers import costs but raises the foreign price of exports, hurting export competitiveness.

questions.q: The mnemonic SPICED (for the effect of a strong pound) stands for:
options: Strong Pound, Imports Cheap, Exports Down
Stable Prices In Currency Exchange Decline
Sterling Price Index Considers Exports Daily
Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer
questions.explain: SPICED - Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer - summarises the effect of a strengthening pound (and reverses for depreciation).

questions.q: Protectionism refers to government measures designed to:
options: Shield domestic industries from foreign competition using tariffs, quotas and subsidies
Force domestic firms to relocate abroad
Encourage free trade by removing all barriers
Fix exchange rates permanently
questions.explain: Protectionism uses tools such as tariffs, quotas and subsidies to protect home industries from imports.

questions.q: A trading bloc is best defined as:
options: A single multinational company operating worldwide
A group of firms that fix prices illegally
A tax imposed on all imported goods
A group of countries that reduce or remove trade barriers between members
questions.explain: A trading bloc is a group of countries that lower trade barriers among themselves to promote trade.

questions.q: A potential drawback for a business of relying on offshoring production to a distant low-cost country is:
options: Guaranteed immunity from exchange-rate changes
Longer, more complex supply chains and possible quality or ethical control problems
Reduced exposure to political risk
Lower transport and communication risks
questions.explain: Offshoring far afield can lengthen and complicate supply chains and make quality and ethical oversight harder.

questions.q: A licensing agreement as a method of international expansion involves:
options: Buying out a foreign competitor
Building wholly owned factories abroad
Merging two firms into one legal entity
Granting a foreign firm the right to produce or sell the product in return for fees or royalties
questions.explain: Licensing lets a foreign partner use the firm's brand, product or process for a fee, a low-cost entry method.

questions.q: In Bartlett and Ghoshal's model, a 'global' strategy is characterised by:
options: No pressure to reduce costs at all
Independent national subsidiaries acting autonomously
Standardised products and centralised operations to maximise efficiency
High local responsiveness and low cost pressure
questions.explain: A global strategy emphasises standardisation and centralisation to exploit scale economies and low cost.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key driver of globalisation?
options: Increased protectionism worldwide
Reduced trade barriers and improved transport and ICT
Rising transport and communication costs
The collapse of containerised shipping
questions.explain: Lower trade barriers together with cheaper transport and ICT have been major drivers of globalisation.

questions.q: The World Trade Organization (WTO) primarily aims to:
options: Increase tariffs between all member states
Manage individual companies' marketing strategies
Promote and regulate freer international trade and resolve trade disputes
Fix global exchange rates
questions.explain: The WTO works to liberalise trade and provides a framework for negotiating and settling trade disputes.

questions.q: An import quota differs from a tariff because a quota:
options: Is a tax that raises import prices
Sets a physical limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported
Subsidises domestic exporters
Has no effect on domestic prices
questions.explain: A quota restricts the quantity of imports allowed, rather than taxing them as a tariff does.

questions.q: In Bartlett and Ghoshal's matrix, a 'multidomestic' strategy is appropriate when there is:
options: High pressure on both dimensions simultaneously
High pressure for cost reduction but low need for local responsiveness
Low pressure on both dimensions
High need for local responsiveness but low pressure for cost reduction
questions.explain: A multidomestic strategy suits markets where local adaptation matters more than global cost efficiency.

questions.q: Comparative advantage, the economic basis for international trade, suggests countries should:
options: Produce everything they can domestically and avoid imports
Only trade with countries using the same currency
Impose tariffs on all imported goods
Specialise in goods they can produce at lower opportunity cost and trade for the rest
questions.explain: The theory of comparative advantage holds that countries gain by specialising where their opportunity cost is lowest and trading.

questions.q: Exporting as a method of entering overseas markets is attractive because it:
options: Always guarantees the highest possible profit margins
Is relatively low-risk and avoids the cost of overseas production facilities
Eliminates the impact of exchange-rate movements
Requires the most capital and commitment of any method
questions.explain: Exporting is a low-commitment, lower-risk entry method since the firm need not build facilities abroad.

questions.q: Free trade between nations is generally argued to benefit consumers by:
options: Guaranteeing every domestic firm survives
Increasing competition, choice and access to cheaper goods
Forcing all firms to produce identical products
Reducing choice and raising prices
questions.explain: Free trade widens consumer choice and tends to lower prices through greater competition and specialisation.

questions.q: A multinational corporation (MNC) is best defined as a business that:
options: Only exports goods from a single home country
Is owned by several national governments
Trades exclusively within one trading bloc
Owns or controls production or service operations in more than one country
questions.explain: An MNC owns or controls value-adding operations in two or more countries.

questions.q: One ethical concern about MNC supply chains in low-income countries is:
options: Over-regulation by the host government
Too much investment in worker safety
Excessively high wages forced on suppliers
Poor working conditions and 'sweatshop' labour at supplier factories
questions.explain: MNCs are often criticised for poor pay and unsafe conditions at supplier factories in developing economies.

questions.q: A foreign direct investment (FDI) decision to locate production abroad is most likely to be influenced by:
options: The colour of the company logo
Only the home country's weather
The personal preferences of customers alone
Factors such as labour costs, infrastructure, proximity to markets and political stability
questions.explain: Location decisions weigh costs, infrastructure, market access, government incentives and political and economic stability.

questions.q: A global (standardised) marketing strategy is most suitable when:
options: Local regulations make a single product impossible
Customer needs are similar worldwide, allowing economies of scale from one approach
Consumer tastes differ sharply between every market
The firm wants maximum local adaptation in each country
questions.explain: Standardised global marketing works best where tastes are broadly uniform, letting the firm exploit economies of scale.

questions.q: If the pound sterling depreciates against the US dollar, UK exporters generally find that their goods become:
options: More expensive in dollars and therefore less competitive
Banned from sale in the United States
Cheaper in dollars and therefore more competitive abroad
Unaffected because exchange rates do not influence trade
questions.explain: A weaker pound lowers the foreign-currency price of UK exports, improving their competitiveness.

questions.q: 'Glocalisation' refers to a strategy in which a business:
options: Sells exactly the same standardised product everywhere
Adapts its global products and marketing to suit local tastes and conditions
Withdraws entirely from foreign markets
Only ever sells in its domestic market
questions.explain: Glocalisation combines global operations with local adaptation of products and marketing.

questions.q: The acronym 'BRICS' refers to a group of major emerging economies that includes:
options: Belgium, Romania, Ireland, Canada, Sweden
Brazil, Romania, Indonesia, China, Singapore
Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa
Britain, Russia, Italy, China, Spain
questions.explain: BRICS stands for Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, fast-growing emerging economies.

questions.q: A customs union differs from a simple free-trade area because a customs union also has:
options: Completely free movement of labour and capital
A common external tariff on goods from non-member countries
A single shared currency by definition
No internal trade at all
questions.explain: A customs union removes internal barriers and adds a common external tariff against non-members.

questions.q: A tariff is best described as:
options: A ban on trading a particular product
A tax placed on imported goods
A physical limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported
A government grant given to exporters
questions.explain: A tariff is a tax on imports, raising their price and protecting domestic producers.

questions.q: One potential benefit of an MNC for a host country is:
options: Job creation and the transfer of skills and technology
A guaranteed reduction in local tax revenue
The automatic transfer of all profits back to the home country with no local benefit
The elimination of all local competition by law
questions.explain: MNCs can bring employment, investment and technology and skills transfer to host nations.
